case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Harvard College’s race-conscious undergraduate admissions process violates Title VI by intentionally discriminating against applicants (including Asian American applicants) and by using race beyond what Supreme Court precedent permits in pursuit of educational diversity, and whether SFFA had and maintained standing to sue.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 U.S.C. § 2000d) (prohibiting race discrimination by recipients of federal funds); and Article III of the U.S. Constitution (standing/mootness doctrines) as a threshold jurisdictional issue.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: SFFA argues that Harvard’s admissions program unlawfully uses race in a manner that constitutes intentional discrimination and racial balancing, penalizing Asian American applicants in particular, and that Harvard’s asserted diversity interest cannot justify the challenged use of race under the strict limits recognized in prior cases (e.g., requiring narrow tailoring and no workable race-neutral alternatives). SFFA also maintains it has associational standing through its members who were affected by Harvard’s admissions practices and that the case is not moot even if individual members’ circumstances changed during litigation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Harvard argues its admissions process fits within the Supreme Court’s permitted framework for limited, holistic consideration of race to obtain the educational benefits of diversity and is narrowly tailored (i.e., race is one factor among many, without quotas). Harvard additionally pressed threshold jurisdictional defenses—arguing at summary judgment that the case became moot because the SFFA members identified as providing standing were no longer in the admissions pipeline or seriously interested in transferring—and later contended the court should have applied a more stringent associational-standing/membership-control inquiry (including “indicia of membership”).
key_precedents: Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin (Fisher II), 579 U.S. 365 (2016)
Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, 438 U.S. 265 (1978)
Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona, 520 U.S. 45 (1997)
WildEarth Guardians v. Public Service Co. of Colorado, 690 F.3d 1174 (10th Cir. 2012)
Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, 346 F. Supp. 3d 174 (D. Mass. 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is stare decisis: Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II permit holistic consideration of race and caution against judicial micromanagement, and reliance interests counsel restraint. But even accepting that framework (as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize), Fisher II makes narrow tailoring an evidence-based burden for the university—requiring workable race-neutral alternatives to be seriously tested, objectives that are sufficiently concrete to permit judicial review, and meaningful limits and an endpoint that prevent drift into racial balancing. On this record, the persistent race-linked effects coupled with objectives that are difficult to measure leave too little for courts to police, so deference risks converting strict scrutiny into a formality. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s categorical Title VI textual argument is powerful, but under my minimalist approach I can resolve the case by applying Fisher II as written and holding Harvard has not carried its narrow-tailoring burden without overruling the diversity precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan rely on Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II to allow “holistic” consideration of race for diversity, but that framework cannot be squared with Title VI’s categorical text forbidding discrimination “on the ground of race” by federally funded programs; as Justice Gorsuch notes, the statute contains no diversity exception. Even accepting coextensiveness with Equal Protection as a matter of precedent, the asserted “educational benefits” interest is not rooted in the Constitution’s original meaning and has proven incapable of judicially manageable limits, inviting racial balancing and stereotyping rather than genuine narrow tailoring. Justice Roberts’s proposal for a narrow Fisher II disposition does not answer the antecedent textual problem: the Court’s diversity carveout lacks any footing in § 2000d’s language, so the proper course is to enforce the statute as written and enjoin intentional race-based admissions. On standing, I agree with the Chief and Justice Alito that SFFA’s associational standing existed at filing and is not mooted by the turnover of individual applicants while the challenged policy remains operative.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—stare decisis and reliance on Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II—does not answer Fisher II’s allocation of the burden: Harvard must produce concrete, reviewable objectives, show workable race-neutral alternatives are insufficient, and demonstrate meaningful temporal limits. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, the combination of amorphous diversity goals and persistent, predictable race-linked outcomes makes it difficult to distinguish this program from impermissible racial balancing, even if labeled “holistic.” Justice Sotomayor is right that disparate outcomes alone do not prove illegality, but strict scrutiny in this setting demands more than assurances of individualized review; the record must supply administrable limiting principles, and it does not. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Title VI textual concerns reinforce my skepticism about indefinite race-based decisionmaking, though I continue to think we can reverse on the narrower Fisher II narrow-tailoring ground without overruling the diversity precedents.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Fisher II demands a rigorous, evidence-based showing of narrow tailoring—measurable objectives, serious consideration of workable race-neutral alternatives, and a meaningful endpoint—and I do not read our precedents as permitting open-ended racial drift. But even accepting that exacting standard, I am not persuaded the record compels the inference Justice Alito draws from persistent race-linked outcomes alone, where the admissions process remains individualized and race operates as contextual information rather than a mechanical determinant or fixed target. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Title VI textual argument (“on the ground of race”) is substantial, yet our longstanding coextensiveness precedents have integrated strict-scrutiny limits into Title VI in this domain, and stare decisis and reliance interests weigh heavily against converting Fisher II’s demanding tailoring inquiry into a categorical bar. Under a pragmatic, real-world lens attentive to access and vulnerability, I would hold Harvard has not been shown—on this record—to have crossed the line into quotas or impermissible racial balancing, though I would require clearer periodic review and endpoint discipline going forward.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s Fisher II narrow-tailoring critique is the closest question: strict scrutiny requires real limits, serious engagement with race-neutral alternatives, and a program that does not devolve into outcome calibration. But Fisher II also cautions against substituting judicial line-drawing for fact-bound assessments of how a holistic process actually operates, and the lower-court findings—crediting individualized review and rejecting quotas—make it hard to say the record compels reversal rather than closer supervision. Justice Thomas’s categorical Title VI textual argument (“on the ground of race”) is forceful, yet adopting it would require repudiating the Court’s coextensiveness line and the settled strict-scrutiny framework without a clear textual necessity, creating administrability and reliance problems inconsistent with a pragmatic textualist approach. I would instead sharpen Fisher II’s limiting principles—periodic review, articulated metrics, and a genuine endpoint—but I do not think the proper appellate posture permits us to declare Harvard’s plan unlawful on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is stare decisis and the coextensiveness line treating Title VI as tracking Equal Protection, but even granting that premise (as the Chief does) Fisher II’s strict-scrutiny demands still require concrete, judicially administrable limits—serious proof that workable race-neutral alternatives are inadequate, plus measurable objectives and an endpoint—and I do not see that burden carried on this record. Justice Sotomayor is right that race-linked outcomes alone do not prove a quota, yet persistent, predictable race effects combined with an amorphous “diversity” objective that cannot be meaningfully assessed makes it impossible to distinguish individualized consideration from forbidden racial balancing or stereotyping in operation. Justice Thomas’s textual argument underscores why reliance interests cannot do the work respondents ask: Title VI’s ban on discrimination “on the ground of race” does not naturally admit an indefinite, ongoing racial thumb on the scale, and precedent cannot supply a limiting principle that the program itself lacks. Accordingly, whether we write narrowly in Fisher II terms (Roberts/Kavanaugh/Barrett) or more directly in Title VI textual terms, reversal remains warranted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the most serious point that Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II permit holistic consideration of race and warn against judicial micromanagement, and I agree stare decisis and institutional stability matter. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Fisher II simultaneously imposes a demanding, evidence-based burden on the university to supply judicially manageable limits—measurable objectives, genuine exhaustion of workable race-neutral alternatives, and meaningful temporal constraints—and Harvard’s record of persistent race-linked effects paired with amorphous diversity metrics makes it difficult to police against impermissible racial balancing. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Title VI textual arguments underscore the gravity of continuing race-based decisionmaking, yet I do not think we must decide the broader statutory question to resolve this case under the existing coextensive strict-scrutiny framework. On the standing point, I remain aligned with the Chief and Justice Kagan that standing is assessed at filing and the ongoing policy keeps the case live.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest argument—stare decisis and reliance on Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II—carries real weight, and I accept (for decision) the coextensiveness framework under Title VI rather than Justice Thomas’s categorical statutory reading. But under Fisher II, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, the university bears an evidentiary burden to articulate sufficiently concrete objectives to permit judicial review, to show no workable race-neutral alternatives would achieve those ends, and to supply a logical endpoint that prevents drift into de facto racial balancing. Persistent, predictable race-linked outcomes do not alone prove a quota (as Justice Sotomayor notes), but combined with objectives framed at a high level of generality and the absence of a clear limiting principle, they make it difficult to verify that race is a last resort rather than a continuing determinant. Because deference cannot substitute for strict scrutiny’s demand for demonstrated tailoring, I would reverse on narrow-tailoring grounds without overruling the diversity precedents.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow-tailoring critique is the most serious: Fisher II requires Harvard to prove, with evidence, meaningful limits, serious consideration of workable race-neutral alternatives, and an endpoint. But under our existing Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II framework—as Justice Kagan emphasizes—those are fact-bound determinations, and the lower courts’ credited findings that Harvard uses race as one contextual factor in individualized review (not as a quota or mechanical balancing) are entitled to weight absent clear error. Justice Alito’s inference of de facto racial balancing from persistent race-linked outcomes does not, standing alone, establish that race is outcome-determinative or that Harvard set targets, especially where other nonracial factors can correlate with race and the process remains individualized. I also cannot join Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s categorical Title VI reading without squarely displacing longstanding coextensiveness precedent and unsettling reliance interests; on this record and posture, I would apply Fisher II as written and affirm.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VI forbids race discrimination by federal-funds recipients, and this Court has treated Title VI’s prohibition as coextensive with the Equal Protection Clause for purposes of evaluating race-conscious admissions under strict scrutiny. Under Fisher II, Harvard bears the burden to show its use of race is narrowly tailored—meaning no racial balancing, sufficiently measurable and limited objectives, and a serious, evidence-based consideration of workable race-neutral alternatives—and the record here indicates Harvard’s program operates with race playing a determinative role beyond what Fisher II permits. On the threshold issue, SFFA maintains associational standing under Article III because it identified members injured by Harvard’s admissions practices, and any later changes in those members’ personal circumstances do not moot a live request for prospective relief where the organization continues to represent similarly situated applicants. A narrow disposition would therefore invalidate Harvard’s challenged admissions use of race under Title VI without reaching broader questions beyond the strict-scrutiny limits already articulated in Fisher II and related cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VI’s text provides that no person, “on the ground of race,” shall “be subjected to discrimination” by any federally funded program, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d; that categorical prohibition forecloses Harvard’s intentional use of race in admissions regardless of asserted educational benefits. Under the original public meaning of “discrimination,” treating applicants differently because of race is unlawful, and this Court’s diversity-driven exceptions in Bakke and Fisher II lack any textual foothold and have proven unworkable, inviting racial balancing and stereotyping. SFFA had and maintained associational standing under Article III because it identified members subject to Harvard’s admissions practices and the case presents a live controversy not mooted by changes in any one member’s circumstances. Accordingly, Harvard’s race-conscious admissions policy violates Title VI and should be enjoined.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VI, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, forbids recipients of federal funds from discriminating on the basis of race, and under our precedents it is coextensive with the Equal Protection Clause’s bar on racial classifications. Justice Powell’s controlling rationale in Bakke permitted only tightly limited, individualized consideration of race to pursue educational diversity, expressly rejecting quotas and racial balancing; Fisher II likewise demanded rigorous narrow tailoring and proof that workable race-neutral alternatives would not suffice. On this record, Harvard’s sustained reliance on race and its measurable racial effects (including adverse treatment of Asian-American applicants) reflect impermissible racial balancing and a lack of meaningful endpoints, exceeding what Bakke/Fisher II allow and thus violating Title VI. SFFA maintained Article III standing through affected members at filing, and Harvard’s later mootness arguments do not defeat jurisdiction because the controversy is capable of continuing to affect members in each admissions cycle and associational standing does not evaporate merely because particular students move through the pipeline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VI’s nondiscrimination mandate is coextensive with equal-protection limits for federally funded universities, and under Bakke, Grutter, and Fisher II a school may consider race as one factor in a holistic process to pursue the educational benefits of diversity, so long as it avoids quotas or racial balancing and shows serious, good-faith consideration of workable race-neutral alternatives. On this record, Harvard’s individualized review—treating race as a contextual factor among many rather than assigning automatic points—fits within the framework Fisher II reaffirmed, and the remedy SFFA seeks would risk serious real-world harm to access and opportunity for historically excluded students. As a threshold matter, SFFA maintained Article III standing because it identified members affected by the challenged admissions practices at filing and the case is not rendered moot merely because individual applicants’ circumstances changed during protracted litigation. Absent a clear showing of intentional discrimination against Asian American applicants or impermissible balancing, Title VI does not compel invalidating Harvard’s limited use of race.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VI’s operative command is nondiscrimination by federally funded programs, and this Court has long treated it as coextensive with Equal Protection analysis in higher-education admissions, allowing a limited, holistic consideration of race to pursue the educational benefits of diversity. Under Fisher II, Harvard’s program is permissible if race is used as one factor among many without quotas or racial balancing, if the university has seriously considered workable race-neutral alternatives, and if the use of race is meaningfully limited and subject to ongoing review—constraints Harvard’s process, as described, can satisfy. On standing, SFFA’s associational standing can rest on identifiable affected members at filing, and later changes in those individuals’ application status do not automatically moot the case where the challenged policy remains in force and the controversy is capable of repetition across admissions cycles. Given the workability and coherence of the Fisher/Grutter framework as applied through Title VI, I would uphold Harvard’s program and reject the jurisdictional objections.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VI’s text provides that no person shall, “on the ground of race,” be “excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination” under a federally funded program, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d—language that admits of no exception for race-based decisionmaking in admissions. Even assuming (as prior cases have) that Title VI tracks the Equal Protection Clause, any race-conscious program must satisfy the strict demands of narrow tailoring, and Fisher II reiterates that universities bear the burden to show workable race-neutral alternatives are insufficient and that race is used only in a limited, time-bound way. On this record, Harvard’s persistent use of race to pursue “diversity” risks precisely the sort of racial balancing and stereotyping our precedents forbid, and the Court should not extend Grutter’s reasoning beyond its already-contested premises. As to jurisdiction, SFFA’s associational standing is satisfied where it identified members injured by the challenged policy at filing, and the case is not mooted merely because particular applicants’ circumstances change during protracted litigation, consistent with Article III principles reflected in Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VI forbids intentional race discrimination by federally funded institutions, and our equal-protection precedents require strict scrutiny with genuine narrow tailoring. Under Fisher II, Harvard bears the burden to show its use of race is necessary, avoids racial balancing, and remains justified in light of workable race-neutral alternatives; the record reflects persistent race-linked effects and an approach that is difficult to square with Fisher II’s requirement of measurable, non-perpetual justification rather than an ongoing racial thumb on the scale. Even accepting Bakke/Grutter’s diversity interest as precedent, Harvard’s program appears to use race in a way that is not sufficiently limited or workable under those constraints, making it unlawful under Title VI. As for jurisdiction, SFFA maintained associational standing under Article III because it identified members affected by the challenged admissions policy and the case presents a live controversy not mooted by changes in individual applicants’ circumstances during litigation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VI’s text bars federally funded institutions from excluding or discriminating against any person “on the ground of race,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, and our cases have long treated that prohibition as coextensive with Equal Protection’s strict-scrutiny limits on racial classifications. Even assuming Grutter/Bakke permit some limited consideration of race, Fisher II requires universities to articulate sufficiently measurable objectives and to prove, with a “demanding” showing, that no workable race-neutral alternatives would achieve the asserted educational benefits and that the use of race is time-limited and narrowly tailored; on this record Harvard’s approach risks functioning as impermissible racial balancing and extends beyond those constraints. As to jurisdiction, SFFA has associational standing because at filing it identified members who were “able and ready” to apply and be subject to the challenged policy, and subsequent changes in individual members’ circumstances do not moot a live challenge to an ongoing admissions regime. Accordingly, Harvard’s use of race violates Title VI as applied under strict scrutiny, and the case is properly justiciable.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VI (42 U.S.C. § 2000d) is coextensive with the Equal Protection Clause in this context, so Harvard’s policy is evaluated under strict scrutiny as articulated in Bakke, Grutter, and Fisher II. On this record, Harvard’s admissions process appears to fit within Fisher II’s framework for a holistic program that treats race as one factor among many, avoids quotas or racial balancing, and is defended as necessary to secure the educational benefits of diversity after serious consideration of race-neutral alternatives. As a threshold matter, SFFA’s standing/mootness objections do not warrant dismissal where the organization identified members allegedly injured by the challenged admissions policy and the controversy remains live despite changes in individual applicants’ circumstances during protracted litigation, consistent with Article III principles reflected in Arizonans for Official English. Given the practical consequences for educational access and the importance of procedural fairness in reviewing complex admissions systems, I would affirm the judgment for Harvard absent a clearer showing of intentional discrimination or impermissible balancing under Title VI.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Harvard’s race-conscious undergraduate admissions program violates Title VI by considering race in a manner that is not narrowly tailored to any permissible educational interest, and whether the case is justiciable (standing/mootness) given changes in SFFA members’ circumstances during litigation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 U.S.C. § 2000d) (as applied to federally funded private universities), with standing and mootness governed by Article III of the U.S. Constitution.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: SFFA argues that Harvard’s holistic admissions process unlawfully discriminates on the basis of race—particularly harming Asian-American applicants—by using race as a meaningful factor, engaging in racial balancing or targets (e.g., “critical mass” concepts), and employing admissions components (such as subjective personal ratings) that function as impermissible racial proxies; SFFA also maintains it has organizational/associational standing through affected members and that the case is not moot despite members aging out of the applicant pool.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Harvard argues its consideration of race is limited and integrated into an individualized holistic review designed to obtain the educational benefits of student-body diversity consistent with Supreme Court precedent (as summarized through Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II); Harvard additionally contends the suit should be dismissed on justiciability grounds, asserting SFFA lacked proper indicia of membership/control for associational standing and that the case became moot because the specific members relied upon for standing were no longer actively applying or seeking transfer, eliminating a live controversy.
key_precedents: Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin (Fisher II), 579 U.S. 365 (2016)
Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, 438 U.S. 265 (1978)
Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona, 520 U.S. 43 (1997) (mootness reference)
WildEarth Guardians v. Public Service Co. of Colorado, 690 F.3d 1174 (10th Cir. 2012) (mootness formulation, cited in the record)

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rely on Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II to read Title VI as permitting “holistic” racial preferences in service of diversity, but that move departs from the statute’s ordinary meaning: a person is “subjected to discrimination” when race is used to allocate benefits or burdens, full stop. Even if those precedents treated Title VI as coextensive with equal protection, that coextensiveness is itself a judicial gloss that cannot override §2000d’s categorical text, and reliance interests cannot justify continuing atextual exceptions. Justice Sotomayor’s deference-based account under Fisher II underscores the problem—once courts accept amorphous ends like “critical mass,” meaningful judicial review collapses into trust, which is incompatible with a strict textual prohibition on race-based discrimination. On justiciability, Justice Gorsuch’s point that associational standing is assessed at filing and that prospective relief targets an ongoing policy confirms that Article III does not require dismissal here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Roberts’s principal point—that Fisher II counsels deference to Harvard’s good-faith holistic judgment and that reliance interests favor adhering to Grutter/Fisher II—does not answer the antecedent statutory problem: Title VI’s command that no person shall, “on the ground of race,” be subjected to discrimination is written in absolute terms, and Harvard concedes race is a meaningful factor in admissions. Even if, as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor contend, Title VI is treated as coextensive with Equal Protection, Harvard still fails narrow tailoring because the asserted “educational benefits of diversity” and “critical mass” are too indeterminate to permit the judicially manageable end Fisher II demands, and they invite the very racial balancing Fisher II and Grutter disavowed. On justiciability, Justice Gorsuch correctly notes standing is assessed at filing under Hunt, and Arizonans for Official English does not require mootness where prospective relief targets an ongoing policy affecting members on a recurring admissions-cycle basis. Practical consequences reinforce the legal conclusion: permitting such an opaque regime entrenches race-based line-drawing and continuous litigation over subjective “holistic” criteria that can operate as racial proxies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point: Title VI’s “no person…on the ground of race” language is facially absolute. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, our Title VI cases from Bakke through Fisher II have repeatedly treated §2000d as coextensive with Equal Protection in higher-education admissions, and that settled construction—administered for decades by universities and agencies—cannot be brushed aside without squarely confronting stare decisis and reliance rather than recasting the statute in this posture. On narrow tailoring, Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh are right to demand rigor, yet Fisher II’s framework provides administrable constraints (individualized review, no quotas/targets, serious race-neutral consideration, and periodic reassessment) without forcing educational judgments into artificial quantification that would effectively make strict scrutiny a disguised per se ban. Under my pragmatic methodology, absent a clearer statutory command or a record showing racial balancing or workable race-neutral substitutes ignored, I would not adopt a rule that predictably curtails access for historically excluded groups and destabilizes the Title VI/Equal Protection alignment we have reaffirmed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best point for Petitioners: Title VI’s ordinary-language prohibition on being “subjected to discrimination” because of race is facially categorical, and Harvard admits race can affect admissions decisions. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that our Title VI line (from Bakke through Grutter and Fisher II) has repeatedly treated §2000d as coextensive with Equal Protection in this precise context, and under our interpretive practice that settled construction is part of what the statute means absent a clear showing it is unworkable or clearly erroneous. Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh’s narrow-tailoring administrability concern about “critical mass” is serious, yet Fisher II supplies judicially manageable constraints (no quotas/targets, individualized review, serious race-neutral consideration, and periodic reassessment), and I do not see this record as establishing a failure under that framework rather than an argument to overrule it. Because Petitioners’ statutory reading effectively requires jettisoning the embedded Title VI/Equal Protection linkage rather than showing Harvard flunks strict scrutiny as we have applied it, I would affirm.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II have treated Title VI as coextensive with Equal Protection and that reliance interests counsel restraint, but settled judicial gloss cannot supply an atextual exception to §2000d’s categorical command that no person be discriminated against “on the ground of race.” Even accepting their coextensiveness premise, Justice Sotomayor’s defense of “critical mass” confirms the narrow-tailoring problem: an elastic objective with no judicially manageable stopping point risks collapsing strict scrutiny into deference and inviting the racial balancing our cases forbid. Justice Jackson’s appeal to agency implementation likewise cannot overcome clear statutory text under separation-of-powers principles; administrative practice cannot amend Congress’s words. On justiciability, I remain aligned with Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh that Hunt measures associational standing at filing and that prospective relief against an ongoing admissions policy is not mooted by turnover among individual applicants.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is institutional: Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II have treated Title VI as coextensive with Equal Protection and reliance interests counsel restraint. But even accepting that coextensive framework (so I need not reach Justice Thomas’s broader textual argument), Fisher II requires a judicially manageable narrow-tailoring inquiry, and Harvard’s “critical mass”–style objectives remain too indeterminate to test necessity, duration, and the availability of workable race-neutral alternatives without collapsing into deference. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of procedural guardrails (individualized review, no quotas, periodic reassessment) helps on means, but it does not supply the concrete endpoint and comparability showing Fisher II demands to prevent the racial balancing those same precedents forbid. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett’s Hunt-at-filing analysis also confirms we can and should reach the merits to enforce that rigor rather than avoid decision on jurisdictional grounds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional point about Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II and reluctance to disrupt the Title VI/Equal Protection linkage is the strongest counterweight, and I accept (for present purposes) Justice Kagan’s view that settled construction bears on statutory meaning. But even within that coextensive framework, Fisher II’s “deference” cannot relieve Harvard of its burden to supply a judicially manageable, time-bounded objective; as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, an elastic “critical mass” goal prevents meaningful narrow-tailoring review and risks devolving into the racial balancing our cases forbid. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on procedural guardrails (no quotas, individualized review, periodic reassessment) answers some concerns, but it does not cure the lack of a concrete endpoint against which necessity and duration can be tested. Because my position rests on Harvard’s failure under strict scrutiny as applied—not on overruling the coextensiveness line—I do not see a new argument that undermines my reasoning.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point: Title VI’s text—“no person…on the ground of race”—sounds categorical, and Harvard concedes race is considered. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan note, Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II have repeatedly treated Title VI as coextensive with Equal Protection in admissions, and that entrenched construction (implemented by agencies and relied upon by universities) is part of what “the law” is unless Congress clearly repudiates it; I do not read §2000d’s general phrasing as an unmistakable command to upend that settled framework. Justice Alito’s and Justice Barrett’s administrability critique of “critical mass” is serious, yet Fisher II’s guardrails supply a procedurally enforceable inquiry (individualized review, no quotas/targets, serious race-neutral consideration, and periodic reassessment), and on this record I do not see the kind of rigid balancing or availability of plainly workable alternatives that would justify declaring the program unlawful wholesale. Under my pragmatic approach, the statutory-text argument here functions as an implicit stare decisis attack, and I am not persuaded the petitioners have shown either clear error or unworkability sufficient to discard the coextensive regime in this posture.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Barrett’s administrability point—grounded in Fisher II’s insistence on rigorous, judicially manageable narrow-tailoring review—genuinely undermines my prior inclination to resolve this case narrowly within the Bakke/Grutter/Fisher II framework. Even accepting, as Justice Kagan urges, that Title VI has long been treated as coextensive with Equal Protection in this domain, that coextensiveness imports strict scrutiny’s requirement of a concrete, testable endpoint; Harvard’s “critical mass”-style objective, on this record, is too indeterminate to permit meaningful review without collapsing into the deference Justice Thomas warns becomes indistinguishable from permission. That conclusion allows us to decide on narrow-tailoring grounds without taking Justice Gorsuch’s invitation to announce a categorical Title VI statutory ban—thus preserving institutional legitimacy while enforcing Fisher II’s demanded rigor. Accordingly, I would reverse on the merits under existing doctrine rather than rewrite Title VI’s meaning.

The suit is justiciable: Title VI, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, supplies the cause of action against a federally funded private university, and the record does not clearly establish that intervening changes in particular applicants’ circumstances render the controversy moot under Article III; at a minimum, the case can be resolved without reaching broader jurisdictional disputes, consistent with Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona. On the merits, our controlling framework—Bakke as implemented by Grutter and most recently applied in Fisher II—permits limited, individualized consideration of race to pursue the educational benefits of diversity, while forbidding quotas or racial balancing. Absent a clear showing that Harvard’s program operates as racial balancing or that workable race-neutral alternatives would achieve comparable diversity benefits with less racial use, Fisher II counsels deference to the university’s good-faith, holistic judgment within strict-scrutiny limits. Given reliance interests and institutional legitimacy concerns, I would adhere to Fisher II’s narrow-tailoring analysis rather than extend Title VI to categorically prohibit Harvard’s approach on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VI provides that no person, on the ground of race, shall “be subjected to discrimination” under any federally funded program, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d; its text admits no exception for “holistic” racial preferences or amorphous goals like “critical mass.” To the extent Regents of the University of California v. Bakke and its progeny (including Fisher II) imported Equal Protection balancing into Title VI, that approach conflicts with the statute’s ordinary meaning and should not control where it authorizes race-based decisionmaking the text forbids. Harvard’s program necessarily makes race a factor in conferring admissions benefits and burdens, which is discrimination under Title VI regardless of asserted educational interests. The suit is justiciable because associational standing does not evaporate merely because particular members’ application status changes during protracted litigation, and in any event claims challenging ongoing admissions policies are not mooted by the passage of time as in Arizonans for Official English.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VI provides that no person shall, “on the ground of race,” be subjected to discrimination under any program receiving federal funds, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, and Harvard’s conceded consideration of race as a meaningful admissions factor is difficult to reconcile with that absolute statutory text. Even assuming (as prior cases have largely done) that Title VI is coextensive with Equal Protection, Harvard’s program still fails narrow tailoring because its asserted “educational benefits of diversity” are too amorphous to permit meaningful judicial review and risk devolving into impermissible racial balancing—concerns this Court warned against even while upholding limited consideration of race in Fisher II. On justiciability, SFFA has associational standing because the challenged admissions policy is ongoing and capable of affecting members each cycle, and the case is not moot merely because particular student-members aged out during litigation, since prospective relief would still redress the organization’s injury and Harvard’s policy remains in force (cf. Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona). Practical consequences also counsel against permitting a regime that invites race-based line-drawing and entrenches perpetual litigation over subjective criteria such as “personal ratings” alleged to function as racial proxies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VI is coextensive with the Equal Protection Clause in this context, so Harvard’s program is lawful if it satisfies strict scrutiny and is narrowly tailored under Bakke/Grutter as elaborated in Fisher II, which permits limited consideration of race within an individualized, holistic review and forbids quotas or racial balancing. On this record as framed, Harvard’s asserted use of race as one factor among many to pursue the educational benefits of diversity fits Fisher II’s narrow-tailoring requirements, including serious consideration of workable race-neutral alternatives and an ongoing obligation to reassess necessity. As to justiciability, SFFA’s associational standing and mootness arguments are not strong enough to defeat jurisdiction where the challenged policy is ongoing and capable of affecting similarly situated members, and the controversy is not rendered moot merely because particular identified students cycle out during litigation. Given the practical consequences for access to opportunity and the remedial harms of a categorical bar, I would affirm that Harvard’s limited, holistic consideration of race is permissible under Title VI and that the case is properly adjudicated.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VI, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, tracks equal-protection principles in this context, so the controlling question is whether Harvard’s limited consideration of race fits within the narrowly tailored, individualized framework this Court approved for higher education in Bakke, Grutter, and Fisher II. On the merits, the record as framed supports that Harvard pursued the educational benefits of diversity through holistic review rather than quotas, and Fisher II requires deference to a university’s reasoned educational judgment while still demanding a serious showing that workable race-neutral alternatives would not achieve comparable diversity benefits. On justiciability, the case remains live where an organization asserts associational standing based on members affected by an ongoing admissions policy and the controversy is capable of persisting through the inherently time-limited admissions cycle, making dismissal for mootness inappropriate under Article III principles reflected in Arizonans for Official English. Given those constraints and the workability/reliance concerns embedded in Fisher II’s application of strict scrutiny, I would affirm Harvard under existing precedent rather than retool the doctrine via Title VI.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VI provides in plain terms that no person, on the ground of race, shall be subjected to discrimination under a federally funded program, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, and that text does not admit a university-created exception allowing race to operate as a plus factor in admissions. Even assuming our equal-protection cases supply the relevant framework, Harvard’s use of race to pursue an amorphous “critical mass” resembles the sort of racial balancing our precedents forbid and cannot be squared with the requirement of narrow tailoring as described in Fisher II and related cases. The case is justiciable because associational standing is evaluated at filing under Hunt, and the injunctive relief sought does not demand individual member participation; later changes in particular members’ applicant status do not erase a live controversy where the challenged policy remains ongoing and capable of affecting members. Consistent with Summers, we must independently ensure Article III is satisfied, but nothing in the record compels dismissal for mootness given the continuing application of Harvard’s admissions program.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VI, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, incorporates the Equal Protection strict-scrutiny framework for federally funded universities, requiring that any use of race be narrowly tailored to a compelling interest. Under Fisher II, the university bears the burden to show with concrete evidence both that its asserted educational benefits of diversity are sufficiently measurable to permit judicial review and that workable race-neutral alternatives would not achieve those benefits; Harvard’s use of race as a meaningful factor coupled with “critical mass”-style objectives and opaque subjective components raises serious narrow-tailoring and workability concerns. On justiciability, SFFA’s associational standing is adequately grounded in members allegedly injured by the admissions policy at filing, and the controversy is not rendered moot simply because particular student-members age out during litigation, consistent with Article III principles and this Court’s mootness guidance in Arizonans for Official English. Given the demanded rigor of Fisher II and the practical need for administrable limits, I would reverse and hold the program violates Title VI.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VI’s text provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the ground of race … be … subjected to discrimination” in federally funded programs, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d, and Bakke’s controlling understanding treats that prohibition as at least coextensive with the Equal Protection Clause’s bar on race-based decisionmaking. Under Fisher II and related precedent, any consideration of race must satisfy strict scrutiny by being narrowly tailored to a concrete, judicially manageable educational interest, yet Harvard’s reliance on amorphous goals like “critical mass” and the practical use of race as a meaningful factor risks functioning as impermissible racial balancing rather than individualized consideration. On justiciability, SFFA’s suit remains live because it seeks prospective relief against an ongoing admissions policy and alleges associational standing through members affected by that policy; the mere passage of time or turnover of particular applicants does not necessarily moot a challenge to a continuing practice. Consistent with Article III limits and Arizonans for Official English, the proper course is to reach the merits where an ongoing policy continues to affect members and the requested relief would redress the alleged injury.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: SFFA has Article III associational standing under Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission because it identified members who would have standing in their own right, the challenge is germane to its purpose, and the prospective injunctive relief sought does not require individualized member participation; changes in particular members’ application status during litigation do not necessarily moot a live, forward-looking dispute where the organization continues to represent similarly situated members and seeks ongoing relief. On the merits under Title VI (42 U.S.C. § 2000d), Harvard’s limited consideration of race within an individualized holistic review can remain permissible when it is narrowly tailored to the educational benefits of diversity as recognized in Bakke and reaffirmed in Fisher II, and where the program is periodically reviewed and does not function as a quota or racial balancing. Given the practical consequences for equal educational opportunity and the need for procedural fairness in evaluating individualized files, I would not hold this record sufficient to deem Harvard’s approach categorically unlawful under Title VI. Accordingly, I would vote to affirm Harvard’s position on both justiciability and the merits.
